chapters.title: Forgive and Forgiveness
chapters.subtitle: In the Bible, forgiveness is a release: a burden lifted, a debt cancelled, a slate wiped clean
chapters.nutshell: The Bible has no single word for “forgive”. Hebrew uses a cluster of vivid pictures: God pardons, lifts and carries sin away, covers it, wipes it out and passes over it. Greek adds the ideas of releasing a captive and cancelling a debt as a free gift. Read through Jewish eyes, forgiveness is not a legal trick that leaves the debt in place; it is a real release that sets people free and restores relationships, with God and with one another.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical forgiveness means God (and we) really let go of what is owed, setting the other person free and restoring the relationship.
skeleton: We often think of forgiveness as a feeling or a legal verdict
Hebrew offers many pictures: pardon, lift, cover, wipe out, pass over
Only God is the subject of salach: true pardon belongs to him
Greek aphesis means release, and echoes the Jubilee year of liberty
In Jesus' Aramaic world, sin is a debt, and forgiving is cancelling it
Jewish tradition joins God's forgiveness to repentance and to making things right with people
Jesus forgives with God's authority and asks us to forgive freely

p: When most of us hear the word **forgive**, we think of one of two things. Either it is a feeling, letting go of anger inside, or it is a legal verdict, where a judge declares a guilty person “not guilty” while the debt is quietly paid by someone else behind the scenes.

The Bible is richer than both. It has no single word for forgiveness. Instead the Hebrew Scriptures use a whole family of word-pictures, and the Greek New Testament adds a few more. Each one shows a different side of the same gift. Looking at them one by one helps us see what God actually does when he forgives, and what he asks us to do for others.

sections.h: Salach: the pardon only God gives
p: The most direct Hebrew word is *salach* (to pardon) and its noun *selichah* (pardon, forgiveness). Something striking stands out: in the Hebrew Bible, **only God is ever the subject of salach**. People ask for it, but God alone gives it.

When Israel rebelled in the wilderness, Moses prayed, “Pardon the iniquity of this people,” and God answered, “I have pardoned, according to your word” (Numbers 14:19–20). The psalmist sings, “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4). Notice the surprising logic: forgiveness does not make people careless about God; it draws them to him in awe and love.

From this word comes *Selichot*, the penitential prayers Jews recite in the days before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and a central blessing of the daily Amidah prayer: “Forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned… Blessed are You, LORD, who is gracious and forgives abundantly.”

The other Hebrew words are pictures taken from everyday life. *Nasa* means to **lift up and carry**. When God reveals his name to Moses, he is the one “forgiving (lifting) iniquity and transgression and sin” (Exodus 34:7). Sin is pictured as a heavy load, and God picks it up and carries it away. Micah asks, “Who is a God like you, lifting iniquity and passing over transgression?” (Micah 7:18).

*Kasah* means to **cover**: “Blessed is the one whose transgression is lifted, whose sin is covered” (Psalm 32:1; see also 85:2). *Kipper*, the Temple word for atonement, means to cover or, more exactly, to purge and cleanse: “On this day atonement shall be made for you, to cleanse you” (Leviticus 16:30).

*Machah* means to **wipe out or blot out**, like wiping a writing tablet clean. David begs, “Blot out my transgressions” (Psalm 51:1, 9), and God promises, “I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins” (Isaiah 43:25). Finally *avar* means to **pass over**, to walk on by without holding the offence against someone (Micah 7:18).

The main New Testament verb is *aphiēmi*, and its noun *aphesis*. The basic meaning is **to let go, release, send away**. The same verb is used for leaving nets, releasing a prisoner, or cancelling a debt. The disciples “left (*aphentes*) their nets” to follow Jesus (Mark 1:18). Forgiveness, then, is not first a feeling; it is **letting something go**.

This word carries a strong Jewish echo. In the Septuagint, the old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, *aphesis* translates the “release” of the Sabbath year and the “liberty” of the Jubilee, when debts were cancelled, slaves were freed and land returned to its families (Leviticus 25:10; Deuteronomy 15:1–2). When Jesus opens his ministry in Nazareth he reads Isaiah 61:1: he has come “to proclaim **liberty** (*aphesis*) to the captives… to set at **liberty** those who are oppressed” (Luke 4:18).
> In Jesus' world, forgiveness and Jubilee are the same word. To be forgiven is to be released: the debt cancelled, the prisoner set free, the inheritance given back.

sections.h: Forgiveness as a gift, a release and a passing over
p: Other Greek words fill out the picture. *Charizomai* comes from *charis*, grace, and means **to give freely, to forgive as a gift**. In Jesus' story of two debtors, the lender “graciously forgave them both” (Luke 7:42–43). Paul uses it when he says, “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32), and “having forgiven us all our trespasses” (Colossians 2:13).

*Apolyō* means **to release or set loose**: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). And *paresis*, used only once, means **passing over**: God in his patience “passed over former sins” (Romans 3:25). This echoes the Hebrew *avar* of Micah 7:18. Every one of these words describes God truly letting go, not simply collecting payment from another source.

sections.h: Sin as a debt: “forgive us our debts”
p: Jesus taught in a world where people spoke Aramaic. In Aramaic the word *ḥova* means both **“debt” and “sin”**. That is why Matthew's version of the Lord's Prayer says, “Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Matthew 6:12), while Luke's version says “sins” and then “everyone who is indebted to us” (Luke 11:4). The two ideas are one.

This shapes how we understand forgiveness. When a lender forgives a debt, nobody pays it; the lender **absorbs the loss** out of generosity. That is the point of Jesus' parable of the unforgiving servant, whose huge debt the king simply cancelled (Matthew 18:23–35). A debt that is forgiven is not a debt that is paid. The servant's failure was not a legal error but a failure to let the mercy he received flow on to others.

sections.h: The Jewish context: teshuvah and Yom Kippur
p: In Jewish thought, forgiveness goes hand in hand with *teshuvah*, “returning” or repentance: turning back to God and to his ways. Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, is the great annual day of cleansing and forgiveness (Leviticus 16:30). Yet the Mishnah adds a famous rule: “For sins between a person and God, the Day of Atonement atones. For sins between a person and their neighbour, the Day of Atonement does not atone until they have made peace with their neighbour” (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).

Jesus says the same thing: “If you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there… First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24). Later Hebrew even has a separate word for the forgiveness people give each other: *mechilah*, “letting go” of a claim, as when a lender waives a debt. Before Yom Kippur, Jews traditionally ask family and friends for *mechilah*.

Because *salach* belonged to God alone, the scribes were shocked when Jesus told a paralysed man, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” They asked, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:5–7). Their question was exactly right from the Hebrew Bible, and that is the point: Jesus was acting with God's own authority, and he proved it by healing the man (Mark 2:10–12).

On the cross Jesus prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). The apostles then proclaimed “forgiveness (*aphesis*) of sins” in his name (Acts 2:38; 10:43). Forgiveness was not only a private transaction; it formed a new community of released people who were to release one another (Colossians 3:13).

English has one main verb for all of this, **forgive**, and translators use it for *nasa*, *salach*, *aphiēmi*, *charizomai* and *apolyō* alike. This is not a mistake. “Forgive” is clear to every reader, and a Bible full of “lifting” and “releasing” would sound strange in English. But the pictures disappear. “Forgiving iniquity” in Exodus 34:7 (KJV, ESV, NIV) is literally **lifting** iniquity, and “whose transgression is forgiven” in Psalm 32:1 is literally “whose transgression is **lifted**”.

The Greek side has the same problem. *Aphesis* becomes “forgiveness” or “remission” in Acts 2:38, but “deliverance” or “liberty” in Luke 4:18. Each choice fits its verse, yet English readers never see that Jesus' Jubilee sermon and the apostles' preaching of forgiveness use **one word**. The KJV's “remission of sins” came through the Latin Vulgate's *remissio*, a word that once meant letting a debt go but now sounds medical.

Romans 3:25 shows how careful translation can recover a lost detail. The KJV said “remission of sins that are past”, blurring Paul's rare word *paresis* with *aphesis*. Most modern versions say God “passed over” (ESV) or “left unpunished” (NIV) former sins, which shows that Paul meant patient **passing over**, the Greek echo of Hebrew *avar*.

Finally, the Lord's Prayer. Matthew's Greek says “debts” and Luke's says “sins”, and good translations keep both. Many English churches pray “trespasses”, a word that comes from William Tyndale's early translation and the Anglican Prayer Book. It is a fine word, but it hides the **debt** picture that Jesus' hearers knew from the Aramaic *ḥova*.

Israel was a land of small farms, heavy loads and written records. People carried water jars, sacks of grain and bundles of wood, so “lifting” a burden was an everyday kindness. Debts were recorded on scrolls and tablets that could be washed or scraped clean. And the Torah built **release** into the calendar: every seventh year debts were to be let go (Deuteronomy 15:1–2), and every fiftieth year the Jubilee returned land to its families (Leviticus 25:10).

Forgiveness was also deeply **communal**. On Yom Kippur the high priest laid his hands on a goat, confessed the sins of the whole people, and the goat “bore” (*nasa*) them away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21–22). In a village culture of honour and shame, being forgiven meant being restored to your place at the family table and in the community, not only feeling better inside.

In the Greco-Roman world, *aphiēmi* and *apolyō* were the language of contracts and courts: cancelling a debt, dropping a charge, releasing a prisoner. *Charis* was the language of **patronage**: a benefactor gave a gift freely, and the receiver responded with loyalty and thanks. So when Paul says “forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave (*charizomai*) you” (Ephesians 4:32), Greek-speaking believers heard of a generous Benefactor whose free gift created a grateful family.

Jesus' own parables come straight out of this world: creditors and debtors (Luke 7:41–43), a king settling accounts (Matthew 18:23–35), a manager reducing debts (Luke 16:1–8). His hearers knew what it was to owe money they could never repay. For them, “release” was not an abstract idea; it was **the best news a debtor could hear**.

Common Western thinking can make forgiveness either a private feeling or a courtroom ruling where someone else is punished in our place. The Jewish lens shows something warmer and more practical: **God really lets go**, and he invites us to do the same. Forgiveness is a release that restores relationships.

This also means forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened. The person who did wrong is called to *teshuvah*: to turn, to apologise and, where possible, to make things right. The person who was wronged is called to release the debt, as God released ours. Ask yourself today: whose debt am I still holding? And is there someone whose forgiveness I need to ask for before I bring my worship to God?

words.note: In the Hebrew Bible only God is ever the subject of this verb.
words.missed: English lets anyone “forgive”, so readers miss that salach is reserved for God, which is why the scribes' question in Mark 2:7 was so sharp.
words.culture: Israel asked for pardon as a covenant people, in the Temple and later in the synagogue, not only as private individuals.

words.note: Gives its name to the Selichot prayers before the High Holy Days.
words.missed: Versions rightly say “forgiveness” in Psalm 130:4, but readers lose the link to the Selichot prayers that Jews still pray.
words.culture: In the weeks before Rosh Hashanah many Jews rise before dawn to recite Selichot together in the synagogue.

words.note: Sin is pictured as a heavy load that God lifts and carries off.
words.missed: “Forgive” in Exodus 34:7 and Psalm 32:1 hides the physical picture: the same verb is used for lifting and carrying a load.
words.culture: People carried water, grain and wood on their backs, so lifting someone's load was a vivid act of help; the Yom Kippur goat “shall bear (nasa) all their iniquities” away (Leviticus 16:22).

words.note: The Temple word for cleansing, at the heart of Yom Kippur.
words.missed: “Atone” (from “at-one”) is a good English word, but it hides the Temple picture of cleansing and purging what sin has defiled.
words.culture: On Yom Kippur the high priest sprinkled blood to cleanse the sanctuary and the people; after the Temple fell, fasting, prayer and repentance took its place.

words.note: Like wiping a writing tablet clean so the record is gone.
words.missed: “Blot out” is close, but modern readers may not hear that it was the word for erasing writing: “blot me out of your book” (Exodus 32:32).
words.culture: Ink on leather or papyrus could be washed off; in Numbers 5:23 a priest writes words and then wipes (machah) them into water.

words.note: God covers sin so that it no longer stands between him and his people.
words.missed: “Cover” can sound like a cover-up; in the psalms it means God no longer looks at the sin or holds it up against us.
words.culture: In an honour-and-shame culture, covering another's shame was an act of kindness (Genesis 9:23), and “love covers all offences” (Proverbs 10:12).

words.note: God walks on by the offence instead of holding it against us.
words.missed: Some versions say “pardons” in Micah 7:18 and lose the picture of walking past an offence without stopping.
words.culture: Where feuds between families could last for generations, to “pass over” a wrong meant refusing to settle the score.

words.note: Later Hebrew word for waiving a debt, used for forgiveness between people.
words.missed: English “forgiveness” mixes God's pardon and people's letting go; later Hebrew keeps them apart with different words.
words.culture: Before Yom Kippur Jews traditionally go to family, friends and neighbours to ask for mechilah face to face.

words.note: In Aramaic the same word means both debt and sin.
words.missed: Translating Matthew 6:12 as “debts” and Luke 11:4 as “sins” is faithful to the Greek, but it splits what was probably one Aramaic word.
words.culture: Many Galilean farmers lived in debt to landowners and feared losing land or family to debt-slavery, so “release of debts” was very good news.

words.note: Also used for leaving nets and cancelling debts.
words.missed: “Forgive” hides that the same verb means “leave” and “let go”, so readers miss the link between leaving nets and letting go of debts.
words.culture: In Greek legal and business documents the verb was used for releasing someone from a debt, a charge or an obligation.

words.note: The Septuagint's word for the Jubilee and Sabbath-year release.
words.missed: English says “liberty” or “deliverance” in Luke 4:18 but “forgiveness” or “remission” in Acts 2:38, so the Jubilee link disappears.
words.culture: Every seventh year debts were to be released (Deuteronomy 15:1–2); by Jesus' day the rabbinic prosbul, credited to Hillel, let lenders still collect (Mishnah Shevi'it 10:3).

words.gloss: to forgive freely, as a gift
words.note: Built on charis, grace: forgiveness is an undeserved gift.
words.missed: “Forgive” hides that this verb is built on charis, gift; the KJV's “he frankly forgave them both” (Luke 7:42) kept a little of the sense of a free gift.
words.culture: In the Greco-Roman world charis was the language of benefactors who gave gifts and of the gratitude owed in return.

words.note: The ordinary word for releasing a prisoner.
words.missed: In Luke 6:37 most versions say “forgive”, but it is the everyday word for releasing a prisoner or dismissing a crowd.
words.culture: Pilate's custom of releasing (apolyō) one prisoner at Passover (Mark 15:6) shows its ordinary legal sense.

words.note: Used only once in the New Testament, echoing the Hebrew avar.
words.missed: The KJV's “remission of sins that are past” (Romans 3:25) blurs paresis with aphesis; most modern versions say God “passed over” or “left unpunished” those sins.
words.culture: In Greek it could describe letting a matter go unpunished for a time, like a ruler postponing a penalty.

The debt is still paid, just by someone else
A private matter between me and God

Nothing to do with repairing harm

right.label: Jewish lens
items: Forgiveness is a release, like the Jubilee

steps.d: A wrong creates a “debt” toward God and often toward a neighbour.
The one who sinned turns back, admits the wrong and seeks to repair it.
God lifts, covers, wipes out and passes over; the debt is cancelled.
Peace is made with the neighbour as well as with God (Matthew 5:23–24).

verses.text: But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.
Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression?
I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.
He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives… to set at liberty those who are oppressed.
And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.
Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.

keyPoints: The Bible uses many word-pictures for forgiveness: pardon, lifting, covering, wiping out and passing over.
In the Hebrew Bible, only God is the subject of salach (to pardon).
Greek aphesis means release and is the same word used for the Jubilee “liberty” (Luke 4:18).
In Aramaic, debt and sin are one word, so forgiving sin is like cancelling a debt.
A forgiven debt is not paid; the forgiver absorbs the loss out of grace.
Jewish teaching (Mishnah Yoma 8:9) and Jesus (Matthew 5:23–24) both say we must make peace with people we have wronged.
Forgiven people are called to forgive others freely.
reflect: Which picture of forgiveness speaks to you most: lifted, covered, wiped clean, or released like a Jubilee slave? Why?
Is there a “debt” someone owes you that you need to release, or someone you need to ask for forgiveness?
How does seeing forgiveness as release rather than payment change the way you think about God?

quiz.q: In the Hebrew Bible, who is the subject of the verb salach (to pardon)?
quiz.why: Salach is used only with God as the one who pardons (e.g. Numbers 14:20; Psalm 130:4).

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word nasa picture?
options: Lifting up and carrying away a load
quiz.why: Nasa means to lift and carry; God “lifts” iniquity (Exodus 34:7; Micah 7:18).

quiz.q: In Luke 4:18, the Greek word aphesis is translated as:
quiz.why: Jesus proclaims aphesis, release, echoing the Jubilee liberty of Isaiah 61:1 and Leviticus 25.

quiz.q: Why does Matthew 6:12 say “debts” where Luke 11:4 says “sins”?
options: One of them made a copying mistake
In Aramaic one word means both debt and sin
quiz.why: The Aramaic word ḥova means both debt and sin, so the two versions say the same thing.

quiz.q: According to Mishnah Yoma 8:9, what must happen for sins against a neighbour?
options: Nothing; Yom Kippur atones for everything
A larger sacrifice must be offered
You must first make peace with your neighbour
Only a rabbi can forgive them
quiz.why: Yom Kippur does not atone for sins against a neighbour until you make peace with them, just as Jesus teaches in Matthew 5:23–24.

quiz.q: Why does the same Greek word aphesis appear as “deliverance/liberty” in Luke 4:18 but “forgiveness/remission” in Acts 2:38?
options: They are two different Greek words
Translators chose the English word that fits each verse, which hides that it is one word
Luke wrote one and someone else wrote the other
quiz.why: Both verses use aphesis, “release”. Each English choice fits its context, but readers lose the link between Jubilee release and forgiveness.

terms.def: Pardon or forgiveness, from salach; in the Bible only God gives it.
To lift up and carry; God lifts sin away like a heavy load.
To wipe out or blot out, as a record is wiped clean.
Release, liberty, forgiveness; also the Septuagint's word for the Jubilee release.
To forgive freely as a gift; related to charis, grace.
Returning or repentance: turning back to God and making things right with others.

chapters.title: Punishment and Discipline
chapters.subtitle: When God corrects, the Bible's words point to a parent training a child and a refiner purifying silver
chapters.trueMeaning: Correction, training and refining that restores
chapters.nutshell: We tend to hear “punishment” as pain paid back for wrongdoing. The Hebrew and Greek words behind it are more varied: God “visits” and attends to wrongs, sin carries its own consequences, discipline is a parent's training, and fire refines silver rather than destroying it. Greek writers even distinguished correction for the sufferer's good from revenge for the punisher's satisfaction. Read through a Jewish lens, God's judgments aim to set things right and to bring people home.
chapters.bigIdea: In the Bible, God's discipline is mainly the loving correction of a parent and refiner, aimed at healing and setting things right.
skeleton: We usually picture punishment as pain paid back
Paqad: God “visits”, attending to wrongs and to people in need
Avon: sin and its consequence are one word
Yasar and musar: discipline is training, like a parent with a child
Tsaraph and shaphat: refining fire and judging that rescues the weak
Greek kolasis, timōria, paideia, dikē and ekdikēsis each add a shade
God's correction comes from love and aims at restoration

p: For many people the word **punishment** means one thing: pain paid back to someone who did wrong, so that justice is “balanced”. If we picture God that way, he can seem like a strict judge who mainly wants each sin repaid.

The Bible's words are wider and warmer. Hebrew and Greek have several different terms that our English Bibles often flatten into “punish”. Some describe a parent training a child. Some describe a metal-worker refining silver. Some describe a judge rescuing the oppressed. Looking at them carefully does not make sin less serious; it shows **why** God deals with it and **what he is aiming at**.

sections.h: Paqad and avon: God attends to wrongs
p: The Hebrew verb *paqad* basically means **to visit, attend to, take note of**. When God “visited” Sarah, he gave her the son he had promised (Genesis 21:1). Joseph told his brothers, “God will surely visit you” and bring you out of Egypt (Genesis 50:24). The same verb is used when God “visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children” (Exodus 20:5; 34:7). God is not indifferent: he attends to wrongs as well as to needs.

Exodus 34:6–7 also sets this in proportion: God is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger,” keeping steadfast love “for thousands”, while the consequences of sin reach “the third and fourth generation”, which many explain as the members of one living household. Mercy is far larger than judgment.

*Avon* means **iniquity**, but it can also mean the **consequence** that grows out of iniquity. When Cain says, “My punishment is greater than I can bear” (Genesis 4:13), the word is *avon*. Hebrew sees sin and its results as one thing: wrongdoing carries its own harm within it, like a seed that grows into its own fruit.

sections.h: Yasar and musar: discipline as training
p: The verb *yasar* and its noun *musar* mean **discipline, instruction, training**. The book of Proverbs opens by saying it was written “to know wisdom and instruction (*musar*)” (Proverbs 1:2). The same word is used for teaching and for correction, because in Hebrew thinking they belong together.

“My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline (*musar*) or be weary of his reproof (*tochachat*), for the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:11–12). Moses says, “As a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you” (Deuteronomy 8:5). *Tochachat* means **correction or rebuke**: showing someone clearly where they went wrong so they can change.
> The picture is not a courtroom but a family. The one who disciplines is a father who delights in his child, and the goal is a wise, mature son or daughter.

sections.h: Tsaraph and shaphat: refining and setting right
p: *Tsaraph* means **to refine or smelt**, the way a metal-worker melts silver to remove the waste. God says of his people, “I will put this third into the fire, and refine them as one refines silver… They will call upon my name, and I will answer them” (Zechariah 13:9). Malachi pictures the Lord sitting “as a refiner and purifier of silver” (Malachi 3:3). Refining fire is painful, but its aim is to **keep the silver and lose the dross**.

*Shaphat* means **to judge**, but in Hebrew judging is mostly about setting things right. “Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute” (Psalm 82:3). A biblical judge was a rescuer, which is why the leaders in the book of Judges were deliverers. When the psalms cry out for God to judge, they are often begging him to come and save.

sections.h: Kolasis and timōria: correction or revenge?
p: In Greek, *kolasis* is the usual word for punishment. Its verb, *kolazō*, first meant to **cut back, prune or check** a plant's growth, and came to mean to correct or punish. *Timōria*, by contrast, meant **retribution**: a penalty that pays back and vindicates the honour of the one who was wronged.

The philosopher Aristotle drew a clear line between them: *kolasis* is inflicted for the sake of the one who suffers it, while *timōria* is for the sake of the one who inflicts it, to satisfy him (Rhetoric 1.10). In the New Testament, *kolasis* appears in Matthew 25:46 (“eternal punishment”) and 1 John 4:18 (“fear has to do with punishment”). *Timōria* appears only once, in Hebrews 10:29 (“how much worse punishment”).

Scholars **debate** how much Aristotle's distinction still applied in the first century; ordinary Greek did not always keep the two words apart. So we should not build a whole doctrine on one word. But it is worth knowing that the word Matthew uses to report Jesus' saying in 25:46 was, in its basic sense, a word for correction.

*Paideia* comes from *pais*, child, and means **child-training, education, discipline**. Hebrews 12:5–11 quotes Proverbs 3:11–12 and explains: “God is treating you as sons… he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness.” Discipline “seems painful rather than pleasant,” but “later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.”

*Dikē* means **justice, or the penalty that justice requires** (2 Thessalonians 1:9; Jude 7). *Ekdikēsis* means **vindication, justice done**, often for the wronged: “Vengeance is mine, I will repay” (Romans 12:19), and God will “give justice to his elect” (Luke 18:7). We leave vengeance to God because only he judges perfectly.

*Basanos* was first a **touchstone**, a dark stone used to test whether gold was real; the verb *basanizō* came to mean to test, then to torment. In Revelation 14:10 it describes torment with fire and sulphur, while in Matthew 14:24 the same verb describes a boat “beaten” by the waves. The word's roots lie in testing and proving.

sections.h: The Jewish context: sufferings of love
p: Jewish tradition took Proverbs 3:12 to heart. The Talmud speaks of *yissurin shel ahavah*, “sufferings of love” (Berakhot 5a): hardships that God allows not to destroy, but to draw a person closer. Lamentations says, “Though he cause grief, he will have compassion… for he does not afflict from his heart” (Lamentations 3:32–33). God takes no pleasure in pain.

Ezekiel puts it plainly: “Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked, declares the Lord GOD, and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23). Even in exile, the prophets always spoke of God's judgments as leading toward return and restoration (Hosea 11:8–9; Jeremiah 29:11–14).

The single English word **punish** stands in for many different words: *paqad*, *avon*, *yasar*, *kolasis*, *timōria* and *dikē*. Translators reach for it because it is clear in context. The NIV's “punishing the children for the sin of the parents” (Exodus 20:5) helps readers who would find the KJV's “visiting the iniquity” puzzling. But “visiting” keeps something precious: the same God who “visits” wrongs also “visited” Sarah with a son (Genesis 21:1). Both choices are honest; each hides something.

*Avon* is a good example of a word that English must split. In Genesis 4:13 most versions say “My punishment is greater than I can bear”, though the word also means “iniquity”, and the verb “bear” is *nasa*, the word for lifting away sin. Some ancient Jewish translations read Cain's words as a confession: “My sin is too great to be forgiven.” The translator has to choose one meaning; the Hebrew holds both.

The KJV's “chastening” and “chastisement” for *musar* and *paideia* were good English in 1611. They come through French from the Latin *castigare*, “to correct, to make pure”. Today they sound like beating. Modern versions (ESV, NIV) say **“discipline”**, which is closer to the training of a child. In the Greek words, *kolasis* and *timōria* both become “punishment”, *dikē* becomes “punished”, and *ekdikēsis* becomes “vengeance”, so English readers cannot see the differences the Greek makes.

In Israel, discipline belonged first to the **family**. Fathers and mothers taught their children at home, “when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way” (Deuteronomy 6:7), and Proverbs is written as a parent speaking to a son. Correction was meant to be private and honest: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but you shall reason frankly with your neighbour” (Leviticus 19:17). Jesus follows the same order: “go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone” (Matthew 18:15).

Public justice happened at the **town gate**, where elders heard cases with witnesses (Ruth 4:1–2). The Torah's system of justice had no prison sentences; the aim was restitution, protection of the weak and the restoring of order. The refining fire of *tsaraph* came from the busy workshops of silversmiths, and the touchstone of *basanos* from the market, where every trader tested coins and gold.

In the Greco-Roman world, *paideia* was the word for education and civilised culture, and every well-off household had a *paidagōgos* to guide its boys. Greek honour culture also knew *timōria*, vengeance that restored a family's honour. And Rome ruled by public penalties: flogging and crucifixion were meant to shame and terrify. Jesus' first hearers lived under that system, which is why the gospel's picture of a Father who disciplines in love sounded so different.

sections.h: Common misunderstandings and living it out
p: A common Western picture treats God's punishment as mainly about satisfying offended honour, with pain as an end in itself. The Hebrew and Jewish lens does not deny that God judges or that sin has real and serious consequences. But it insists that God judges **as a father, a refiner and a rescuer**: to stop evil, defend the weak, and bring his children home.

This matters for how we live. When hardship comes, we can ask what God may be teaching, without assuming he is angry with us. When we correct our own children, students or friends, our goal should be their growth, not our satisfaction. And when we are wronged, we can leave justice in God's hands, trusting him to set things right (Romans 12:19–21).

words.note: God attends to people's needs and to their wrongs alike.

diagrams.title: What is punishment for?
diagrams.note: Different words sit at different points; most of the Bible's vocabulary leans toward correction and restoration.

verses.text: My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline or be weary of his reproof, for the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights.
As a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you.
He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver.
He disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness… later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.
Though he cause grief, he will have compassion… for he does not afflict from his heart.
Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked… and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?

keyPoints: English “punish” covers many different Hebrew and Greek words with different shades of meaning.
Paqad means God “visits” or attends to things, both in blessing and in judgment.
Avon means both sin and its consequence: wrongdoing carries its own harm.
Musar and paideia mean discipline as a parent's training, given in love (Proverbs 3:11–12; Hebrews 12:5–11).
Refining fire (tsaraph) removes waste but keeps the silver.
Classical Greek distinguished kolasis (correction for the sufferer) from timōria (payback); how far this applies in the New Testament is debated.
God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked; his aim is that people turn and live.
reflect: Have you ever experienced a hard season that later “yielded the peaceful fruit of righteousness”? What did you learn?
When you correct others, is your aim their growth or your own satisfaction?
How does picturing God as a refiner rather than an executioner change the way you pray?

quiz.q: What is the basic meaning of the Hebrew verb paqad?

Kolasis is for animals, timōria for people
Kolasis is eternal; timōria is temporary

options: To remove the waste and keep the silver pure

Because the KJV mistranslated the verse

chapters.title: Flesh and Body
chapters.subtitle: The Bible does not teach that the body is bad and the soul is good
chapters.trueMeaning: Frail human life, kinship, the whole person
chapters.nutshell: In Hebrew, “flesh” (basar) means the body, human weakness, family ties and even all living creatures. It is not evil: God promises a “heart of flesh” and to pour out his Spirit “on all flesh”. Jews saw a person as one living whole, with a struggle between good and evil inclinations, not between a bad body and a good soul. When Paul contrasts “flesh” and “Spirit”, he means human life lived by its own strength versus life led by God's Spirit, not body against soul.
chapters.bigIdea: Biblical “flesh” is frail human life, not an evil body; the body is good, and the real struggle is between living by our own power and living by God's Spirit.
skeleton: Many Christians assume the body is bad and the soul is good
Hebrew basar means body, frailty, kinship and “all people”
Flesh can be good: a heart of flesh, the Spirit on all flesh
Nefesh is the whole living person, not a soul trapped in a body
Jewish teaching sees a struggle of two inclinations, not of body and soul
Greek sarx and sōma: the Word became flesh, the body is God's temple
Paul's “flesh vs Spirit” matches the Jewish two-inclinations picture
Living it out: honouring the body, walking by the Spirit

p: Many Christians grow up with a quiet assumption: the **body** is the problem and the **soul** is what really matters. The body has desires that drag us down, while the soul is pure and will one day escape to heaven. When we read Paul's warnings about “the flesh”, it seems to confirm this picture.

That picture owes more to Greek philosophy than to the Bible. Thinkers like Plato taught that the body was a kind of prison for the soul. The Hebrew Scriptures, and the Jewish world of Jesus and Paul, saw things very differently. To read Paul well, we need to start with the Hebrew word *basar*.

*Basar* literally means **flesh**, the soft tissue of the body, and by extension the **body** itself. But it is used in several wider ways. It means **kinship**: when Adam sees Eve he says, “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23), and Laban tells Jacob, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh” (Genesis 29:14). Husband and wife become “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).

It means **human frailty**: “All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field” (Isaiah 40:6). God “remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again” (Psalm 78:39). It means **all people, or all living creatures**: “the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together” (Isaiah 40:5).

Flesh is weak, but it is not wicked. The psalmist asks, “What can flesh do to me?” (Psalm 56:4), and Jeremiah warns against the one who “makes flesh his strength” and turns from the LORD (Jeremiah 17:5). The problem is not having a body; it is **relying on mere human strength instead of God**.

sections.h: A heart of flesh and the Spirit on all flesh
p: Sometimes *basar* is even a word of hope. God promises, “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). Here flesh means a heart that is soft, alive and able to respond, in contrast to a cold, hard stone.

Joel declares, “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28; 3:1 in Hebrew Bibles), and Peter quotes this at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). God's Spirit does not avoid flesh; he fills it. A related word, *she'er*, also means **flesh or meat** and, like *basar*, a **close blood relative**: “None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives” (Leviticus 18:6, literally “the *she'er* of his flesh”).

English Bibles often translate *nefesh* as “soul”, which makes us think of an invisible part living inside the body. But in Genesis 2:7, God forms the man from dust, breathes into him the breath of life, and “the man became a living *nefesh*”. He did not *receive* a soul; he *became* one. *Nefesh* is **the whole living person**, a breathing, hungry, feeling creature. Animals too are called living *nefesh* (Genesis 1:24).

So in Hebrew thinking a human being is **a unity**: body, breath, heart and mind together. There is no picture of a good soul trapped in an evil body. Jewish morning prayers even thank God for the body's workings in the blessing *Asher Yatzar*, praising the One who “formed the human being with wisdom”.

sections.h: The two inclinations: the Jewish picture of the struggle
p: If the body is not the enemy, where does the struggle with sin come from? Jewish tradition speaks of two inclinations in every person: the *yetzer hara*, the **evil inclination**, and the *yetzer hatov*, the **good inclination**. The idea is rooted in Genesis, where God sees that “every intention (*yetzer*) of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Genesis 6:5; see 8:21).

The Mishnah reads “love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:5) as “with both your inclinations, the good and the evil” (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5). In other words, even our strong drives are to be directed toward loving God. A well-known midrash even says that without the evil inclination nobody would build a house, marry or have children. The drives are not evil in themselves; they must be **ruled and guided**.
> The battle is not body against soul. It is the whole person pulled between two directions: toward self or toward God.

sections.h: Sarx, sōma and the Word made flesh
p: In Greek, *sarx* is the Septuagint's usual word for *basar*. Its most famous use is shocking for anyone who thinks flesh is evil: “**The Word became flesh** and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). John even warns that denying “Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” is a sign of false teaching (1 John 4:2). Paul can also use *sarx* neutrally: “the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God” (Galatians 2:20).

*Sōma* means **body**, and Paul speaks of it with great honour: “Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:19); “present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). The body will not be thrown away but raised: “It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44). *Kreas* simply means **meat** for eating (Romans 14:21; 1 Corinthians 8:13), and *psychē*, like *nefesh*, usually means **life** or the living self (Mark 8:35).

When Paul sets “flesh” against “Spirit” (Romans 8:4–9; Galatians 5:16–24), he is using *sarx* in a special sense: **human life lived by its own power, cut off from God's Spirit**. Look at his list of “the works of the flesh”: alongside sexual sins he names “enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy” (Galatians 5:19–21). Most of these are not bodily sins at all; they are sins of pride and broken relationships.

This is why some translations that render *sarx* as “sinful nature” can mislead. They can suggest that the body, or some separate part of us, is evil by nature. Paul's picture is much closer to the Jewish two inclinations: the whole person can follow a self-centred direction or be led by God's Spirit. Even “nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7:18) describes human life on its own, without God's power, not the body as evil.

sections.h: Western misunderstandings and the Jewish lens
p: When the church moved into the Greek world, some groups, later called **Gnostics**, taught that matter and the body were evil and that salvation meant the soul escaping the body. The early church rejected this. It confessed that God created the material world good, that the Word truly became flesh, and that believers look forward to “the resurrection of the body”.

Yet the Greek picture has often crept back in, making Christians ashamed of their bodies or indifferent to physical needs. The Jewish lens corrects this: God made the body, Jesus took on a body, the Spirit lives in our bodies, and God will raise our bodies. The struggle is real, but it is about **which direction the whole person follows**.

The word *nefesh* shows how a long chain of translation can shape our thinking. The Septuagint rendered it *psychē*, the Latin Vulgate *anima*, and English “soul”. Each step was reasonable, but by the time it reached English, “soul” carried centuries of Greek philosophy: an invisible, immortal part living inside the body. So when the KJV says “man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7), readers imagine something added. Modern versions say **“a living being”** (NIV) or “a living creature” (ESV) to recover the Hebrew picture of the whole breathing person.

The same word can even be translated two ways in one sentence. In Mark 8:35–36 the KJV says “whosoever will save his **life** shall lose it” and then “lose his own **soul**”, though Jesus uses *psychē* both times. Translators change words for good English style, but readers may think Jesus has moved from earthly life to the afterlife, when he is speaking of **one self** that can be saved or lost.

With *sarx*, translators face a real problem: in modern English “flesh” sounds like skin and muscle, and Paul clearly does not mean the body is evil. So the 1984 NIV and the NLT chose “sinful nature”. The aim was good, but “nature” can suggest a fixed evil part of us, and it hides the link with “the Word became flesh”. The 2011 NIV mostly returned to “flesh”, as the ESV, NASB and NRSV do, and readers must learn its meaning from context.

Finally, *basar* in “all flesh” becomes “all people” in the NIV (Isaiah 40:5; Joel 2:28). That is clear and correct, but it loses the bodily, fragile picture: God's glory is seen by frail creatures, and his Spirit is poured out on **flesh**.

In an Israelite village, a person belonged to a household, a clan and a tribe, and family was described in bodily terms: “my bone and my flesh”. Land, name and inheritance passed through these bonds. Meat was precious and usually eaten at a sacrifice or a feast, so *basar* on the table meant celebration, and the body was something to be washed, clothed, fed and finally buried with one's ancestors.

Jewish life has always honoured the body. Every morning the blessing *Asher Yatzar* thanks God for the body's workings; the dead are buried, not burned, in hope of the resurrection (Daniel 12:2); and marriage and children are seen as a command and a blessing (Genesis 1:28). There was no ideal of escaping the body to become spiritual.

The Greek world Paul wrote to felt differently. Plato reported the saying that the body (*sōma*) is a tomb (*sēma*) for the soul, and many educated people thought of the flesh as low and the soul as divine. At the same time cities honoured athletes in the gymnasium and sold temple-offered meat in the market. Into this world Paul brought a Jewish message: the body is the Spirit's temple, and **God will raise it**.

If the body is a temple, we honour God by caring for it: rest, food, work and touch are not unspiritual. If “all flesh” is frail like grass, we can be gentle with human weakness, our own and others'. And if “flesh” in Paul means life lived by our own strength, then the answer is not hating our bodies but **walking by the Spirit** (Galatians 5:16), letting God's Spirit produce “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23) in our everyday, bodily lives.

words.note: Weak but not evil; “all flesh” means all people or all creatures.
words.missed: English “flesh” sounds either like meat or like sinful desire, so basar's warm senses of family and human frailty are easily lost.
words.culture: Meat (basar) was eaten mainly at feasts and sacrifices, and a person's identity came from the household and clan, their “bone and flesh”.

words.note: Like basar, it can mean a close family member.
words.missed: Translations rightly say “close relative” in Leviticus 18:6, so readers do not see it is a word for flesh and meat (Psalm 78:27 “he rained flesh”).
words.culture: The marriage laws of Leviticus 18 protected the household by forbidding unions with one's “near flesh”.

words.note: The man did not receive a nefesh; he became one.
words.missed: The KJV's “a living soul” (Genesis 2:7) makes readers picture an invisible part inside; the ESV says “a living creature” and the NIV “a living being”.
words.culture: Nefesh first means throat or breath (Isaiah 5:14 “Sheol has enlarged its appetite”); in a hot, dry land, thirst and breath were the plainest signs of life.

words.note: God's Spirit is poured out on flesh, not kept away from it.
words.missed: English must choose “wind”, “breath” or “spirit”, but Hebrew hears all three at once, as in Ezekiel 37.
words.culture: In a land that depended on rain, the west wind from the sea brought life, while the east wind from the desert withered crops.

words.note: The pull toward selfishness and sin in every person.

words.culture: The rabbis pictured life as a lifelong struggle in which Torah study, prayer and good habits help a person rule the evil inclination.

words.note: The pull toward God and goodness; both are to serve love for God.
words.missed: Western theology often speaks of a single “sinful nature”, which loses the Jewish picture of two pulls inside the same person.
words.culture: Jewish tradition teaches that the good inclination grows strong as a child reaches maturity, around the age of bar mitzvah.

words.gloss: flesh; human life on its own
words.note: The Septuagint word for basar; in Paul often life apart from God's Spirit.
words.missed: The 1984 NIV and the NLT often render sarx “sinful nature”; the 2011 NIV mostly returned to “flesh”, because “nature” can suggest a fixed evil part of us.
words.culture: In Greek philosophy flesh was often despised as the soul's prison; Paul uses the word in a Jewish way, for human life without God's Spirit.

words.note: The body is good, a temple of the Spirit, and will be raised.
words.missed: “Body” is accurate, but readers shaped by Greek ideas may hear “shell”; Paul's sōma is the whole person living in the world.
words.culture: Greek cities admired the athlete's body, yet many thinkers hoped the soul would escape it; Paul's teaching on bodily resurrection made Athenians laugh (Acts 17:32).

words.note: Flesh as food, with no moral meaning.
words.missed: Older English used “flesh” for meat (KJV “It is good neither to eat flesh”, Romans 14:21), which can be confused with Paul's moral “flesh”.
words.culture: In Greek cities much of the meat sold in the market (makellon, 1 Corinthians 10:25) had first been offered in a temple, which is why meat troubled the Corinthians.

words.note: Usually the Greek for nefesh: the whole life, not a ghost inside.
words.missed: Translators switch between “life” and “soul” for the same word (Mark 8:35–36 KJV), so readers miss that Jesus is speaking of one thing.
words.culture: Platonic thinking made psychē an immortal soul that leaves the body; in Jewish Greek it usually translated nefesh, the living self.

rows.literal: and the man became a living nefesh (a breathing, living being)
rows.common: man became a living soul (KJV); “a living being” (NIV)
rows.why: “Soul” came down through Greek psychē and Latin anima; modern versions changed it so readers do not picture a separate ghost inside.

rows.literal: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh
rows.common: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh (KJV); “on all people” (NIV)
rows.why: “All people” is clearer, but it loses the striking picture of God's Spirit filling frail human flesh.

rows.literal: every shaping (form) of the thoughts of his heart
rows.common: every imagination of the thoughts of his heart (KJV); “every inclination” (NIV)
rows.why: “Imagination” (from Latin imago, image) is not far from yetzer, something formed in the mind; “inclination” stresses its pull.

rows.literal: you will not carry out the desire of the flesh
rows.common: ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh (KJV); “the desires of the sinful nature” (NIV 1984)
rows.why: “Sinful nature” tried to show Paul did not mean the body, but it can suggest an evil part of us; the 2011 NIV returned to “flesh”.

rows.original: ὃς γὰρ ἐὰν θέλῃ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ σῶσαι… ζημιωθῆναι τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ
rows.literal: whoever wants to save his psychē… to forfeit his psychē
rows.common: save his life… lose his own soul (KJV)
rows.why: The KJV uses “life” in verse 35 and “soul” in verse 36 for the same word, so readers think Jesus changes subject.

left.label: Greek dualism
items: Body is bad, soul is good
Salvation is the soul escaping the body
Flesh means the physical body
Sin comes from bodily desire
The body is thrown away at death

right.label: Jewish lens
items: The whole person is one living unity
Salvation includes the resurrection of the body
Flesh means frail human life, often without God
Sin comes from a misdirected inclination of the heart
The body is God's temple and will be raised

children: Opposite of walking by the Spirit

verses.text: Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.
And all flesh shall see it together… All flesh is grass.
I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.
And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?
Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.

keyPoints: Hebrew basar means body, kinship, human frailty and “all people”; it is weak but not evil.
God promises a “heart of flesh” and pours out his Spirit “on all flesh”.
Nefesh is the whole living person: the man “became a living nefesh” (Genesis 2:7).
Jewish teaching locates the struggle in two inclinations, not in body versus soul.
The Word became flesh, the body is a temple of the Spirit, and it will be raised.
In Paul, “flesh” often means human life by its own power; many “works of the flesh” are not bodily sins at all.
“Sinful nature” can mislead if it suggests the body is evil; the Gnostic view was rejected by the early church.
reflect: Have you ever felt that your body was “unspiritual”? How does John 1:14 challenge that?
Looking at Galatians 5:19–23, which “work of the flesh” and which “fruit of the Spirit” most need attention in your life?
How could you honour God this week with your body as well as your thoughts?

quiz.q: When Laban says to Jacob, “You are my bone and my flesh” (Genesis 29:14), what does “flesh” mean?
quiz.why: Basar often expresses kinship, as also in Genesis 2:23.

options: Received a soul into his body
Was given a body as a prison
quiz.why: He became a living nefesh: a whole living person, not a soul placed in a container.

quiz.q: Jewish tradition describes the inner struggle as a conflict between:
options: The yetzer hara and the yetzer hatov
quiz.why: Jewish teaching speaks of the evil and good inclinations, rooted in Genesis 6:5 and 8:21.

quiz.q: Which of these does Paul list among “the works of the flesh” in Galatians 5:19–21?
quiz.why: Many works of the flesh, such as jealousy, strife and divisions, are not bodily sins, showing that flesh means more than the body.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about the body in 1 Corinthians 6:19?
options: It is a prison for the soul
It does not matter to God
It is a temple of the Holy Spirit
quiz.why: The body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:44).

quiz.q: Why did some translations render Paul's sarx as “sinful nature”?
options: To show that Paul did not mean the physical body is evil
Because the Septuagint used that phrase
Because Paul never used the word “flesh”
quiz.why: Translators wanted to avoid the idea that the body is evil, but “nature” can suggest a fixed evil part of us; many versions keep “flesh”.

terms.def: Flesh or body; also kinship, human frailty and all living beings.
A living being; the whole person, often translated “soul”.
The evil inclination: the inner pull toward selfishness and sin.
The good inclination: the inner pull toward God and goodness.
Flesh; in Paul often human life lived by its own power apart from God's Spirit.
Body; good, a temple of the Spirit, and destined for resurrection.
